passages.text: Beyond One-Size-Fits-All: Individually Tailored Dietary Interventions in Modern Obesity Care

Obesity is a complex, multifactorial chronic disease characterized by excessive and/or aberrant adiposity that requires interventions beyond conventional calorie-restriction models. <sentence_start/>Current clinical guidelines converge on behavioral modification, encompassing nutritional therapy, physical activity, stress reduction, and sleep improvement, as the cornerstone of obesity management, with psychological therapy, pharmacotherapy, and bariatric procedures as adjunctive or escalating options. <sentence_start/>While traditional “one-size-fits-all” dietary approaches frequently yield suboptimal long-term outcomes, precision nutrition has emerged as a promising strategy for individualized obesity care. <sentence_start/>This review critically appraises the evidence underlying each pillar of precision nutrition: genetic profiling shows clear utility in monogenic obesity but variable benefit when diet is matched to common polygenic variants; microbiome-targeted studies reveal that the <italic>Bacillota</italic> to <italic>Bacteroidota</italic> ratio shows inconsistent associations with obesity across studies, with genus-level and functional alterations offering more reproducible targets; and metabolomic profiling of postprandial glycemic responses has progressed from foundational predictive algorithms to large-scale clinical validation. <sentence_start/>It also highlights chrono-nutrition, the alignment of food timing with individual chronotype, as an emerging pillar of personalization. <sentence_start/>Beyond dietary composition, the review addresses how personalized nutrition can mitigate the adverse effects of incretin-based pharmacotherapy and discusses how artificial intelligence can integrate multi-omics and behavioral data into real-time dietary guidance. <sentence_start/>Future clinical implementation will require overcoming challenges related to data integration, predictive accuracy, and accessibility, paving the way for more effective, evidence-based obesity management.
1. Introduction

Obesity represents a major global health issue characterized by excessive and/or aberrant adiposity that significantly impairs physical health, quality of life, and life expectancy. <sentence_start/>The rising prevalence of obesity and its associated non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, emphasize the urgent need for effective therapeutic strategies [<citation rid="B1-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/biomedicines13020502" pmid="40002915" pmcid="PMC11853126" count="1">1</citation>,<citation rid="B2-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00424-025-03066-8" pmid="39924587" pmcid="PMC12003543" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Current management guidelines converge on behavioral modification, encompassing nutritional therapy, physical activity, stress reduction, and sleep improvement, as the foundational cornerstone of obesity care, with psychological therapy, pharmacotherapy, and metabolic or bariatric procedures (surgical and endoscopic) considered as adjunctive or escalating options for patients who do not achieve sufficient benefit from lifestyle intervention alone [<citation rid="B3-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-024-03095-3" pmid="38969880" count="1">3</citation>].

Historically, weight management has relied heavily on the “calories in, calories out” framework and standardized dietary interventions. <sentence_start/>However, this conventional “one-size-fits-all” approach often fails to achieve sustainable weight loss due to substantial interindividual differences in metabolic responses, driven by variability in genetic predisposition, body composition, insulin sensitivity, hormonal fluctuations, and lifestyle habits (e.g., exercise, sleep, stress) [<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms252413438" pmid="39769203" pmcid="PMC11676201" count="1">4</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In recent years, the paradigm of obesity care has shifted towards precision nutrition, an approach that tailors dietary recommendations to an individual’s unique biological and lifestyle characteristics. <sentence_start/>By capitalizing on advances in omics technologies, including genomics, metabolomics, and microbiomics, precision nutrition seeks to identify the specific drivers of metabolic dysfunction in each patient [<citation rid="B5-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00508-022-02146-4" pmid="36717394" pmcid="PMC10020295" count="1">5</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Concurrently, the advent of highly effective incretin-based pharmacotherapies, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, has revolutionized clinical obesity management. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, these pharmacological treatments present new nutritional challenges, requiring personalized dietary strategies to manage gastrointestinal adverse effects, prevent nutritional deficiencies, and preserve lean body mass [<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/15598276251344827" pmid="40452753" pmcid="PMC12125019" count="1">6</citation>].

Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offers unprecedented opportunities to analyze complex multi-omics data, enabling dynamic, individually tailored nutritional interventions. <sentence_start/>Recent progress in AI for precision nutrition has expanded across domains such as dietary assessment, phenotyping, risk prediction, and the generation of personalized dietary recommendations. <sentence_start/>By using ML algorithms to decipher intricate genomic and metabolic data, AI has the potential to translate complex biological information into actionable, real-time nutritional guidance, ultimately paving the way for more sustainable and effective obesity management [<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms252413438" pmid="39769203" pmcid="PMC11676201" count="1">4</citation>].

This review aims to comprehensively evaluate the limitations of traditional dietary models and delineate the core pillars of precision nutrition, highlighting its integration with modern pharmacotherapy and the transformative potential of AI in advancing individualized obesity care.
2. Methodology

The present manuscript is a non-systematic, state-of-the-art narrative literature review synthesizing the current knowledge on the individualized management of obesity. <sentence_start/>As a narrative review, this work does not follow a PRISMA-based protocol, was not registered in advance, and does not report a quantitative synthesis (e.g., meta-analysis) of the retrieved evidence. <sentence_start/>Instead, it provides a critical, integrative overview of the field intended to contextualize and interpret the existing literature. <sentence_start/>A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, covering publications from January 2017 to June 2026.

A wide range of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms were utilized to ensure thorough coverage, including but not limited to: obesity, precision nutrition, personalized nutrition, individualized dietary interventions, genetics, nutrigenetics, genome-wide association studies (GWAS), gut microbiome, probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, metabolomics, lipidomics, incretin-based pharmacotherapies, GLP-1 receptor agonists, dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, weight management, interindividual variability, caloric restriction, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. <sentence_start/>Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) were systematically applied to refine and optimize the search strategy across all databases. <sentence_start/>The inclusion criteria were: (1) peer-reviewed original research articles, clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and narrative reviews published in English between January 2017 and June 2026; (2) articles addressing the pathophysiology of obesity and the mechanisms underlying interindividual variability in responses to diet; (3) publications exploring omics-based approaches in the context of personalized obesity management; (4) studies examining the nutritional implications and dietary optimization strategies associated with incretin-based pharmacotherapies; and (5) publications investigating the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning in precision nutrition and obesity care.

Scientific articles were first analyzed based on their titles and abstracts to establish relevance to the review’s scope. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, full-text evaluations were performed for all articles meeting the inclusion criteria. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, epidemiological data were obtained from the official websites of relevant international health organizations and regulatory agencies. <sentence_start/>The findings were critically synthesized to present an integrated, up-to-date perspective on the individually tailored dietary interventions in modern obesity care.

To improve the transparency and reproducibility of the search and selection process, a PRISMA-inspired flow diagram summarizing the number of records identified, duplicates removed, records screened, full-text articles assessed, and studies ultimately included is presented in Figure 1. <sentence_start/>It should be noted that, in agreement with the non-systematic nature of this narrative review, the selection process was not guided by a pre-registered protocol, and articles were included based on thematic alignment as deemed by the authors rather than a standardized, reproducible screening algorithm applied independently by multiple reviewers.
3. <sentence_start/>The Global Burden of Obesity

Obesity has become a global epidemic, standing out as one of the major health crises of the 21st century [<citation rid="B7-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.metop.2025.100375" pmid="41041606" pmcid="PMC12486175" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>According to the World Health Organization (WHO), between 1990 and 2022, adult obesity rates more than doubled, while in children and adolescents, the prevalence has quadrupled, outpacing the rate of increase seen in adults. <sentence_start/>Formerly seen as a challenge for high-income countries alone, obesity now extends across all regions of the world, affecting people of every socioeconomic background. <sentence_start/>In 2022, approximately one in eight people worldwide lived with obesity, accounting for nearly 880 million adults and about 159 million children and adolescents [<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="B9-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">9</citation>].

In the United States specifically, obesity prevalence rose dramatically, reaching 40.3% among adults between 2021 and 2023 [<citation rid="B10-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15620/cdc/159281" pmcid="PMC11744423" pmid="39808758" count="1">10</citation>,<citation rid="B11-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A similar pattern is observed in Europe, where around 59% of adults live with overweight or obesity, representing a major risk factor for NCDs [<citation rid="B12-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These trends are expected to worsen globally: projections from the World Obesity Atlas suggest that by 2030, the number of adults living with obesity will exceed 1.13 billion, and by 2040, childhood obesity will surpass childhood underweight globally [<citation rid="B13-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="B14-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>].

Beyond these projections, it is important to acknowledge that obesity already represents a serious threat to public health, substantially increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, dyslipidemia, hypertension, at least 13 distinct cancers, obstructive sleep apnea, and osteoarthritis [<citation rid="B15-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the case of type 2 diabetes, the American Diabetes Association (ADA) emphasizes that obesity is a primary driver of the disease, accounting for up to 53% of new cases every year in the United States [<citation rid="B16-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, obesity acts as a risk factor for infection-related hospitalizations and death across a wide range of pathogens, populations, and clinical backgrounds [<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0140-6736(25)02474-2" pmid="41679324" pmcid="PMC12979006" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The magnitude of this burden is highlighted by epidemiological data: in 2019, a high body mass index (BMI) was responsible for approximately 5 million deaths globally. <sentence_start/>In the WHO European Region alone, overweight and obesity accounted for more than 1.2 million deaths annually, making them the fourth leading NCD risk factor in the region, after hypertension, diet quality, and tobacco use [<citation rid="B7-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.metop.2025.100375" pmid="41041606" pmcid="PMC12486175" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="B12-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">12</citation>,<citation rid="B15-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">15</citation>].

Obesity reduces life expectancy and significantly diminishes quality of life. <sentence_start/>The financial impact is staggering, with projections indicating that the worldwide economic burden of overweight and obesity could rise to US$4.32 trillion per year by 2035. <sentence_start/>This emphasizes the urgent need for effective, sustainable, and individualized public health and clinical interventions [<citation rid="B7-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.metop.2025.100375" pmid="41041606" pmcid="PMC12486175" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="B18-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34283488" count="1">18</citation>].
4. <sentence_start/>The Current Definitions of Obesity

Obesity is recognized as a chronic, complex condition characterized by an excessive and/or aberrant accumulation of fat, which can detrimentally impact both physical health and overall quality of life [<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Traditionally, the main approach for identifying overweight and obesity has been the BMI, determined by dividing a person’s weight in kilograms by the square of their height in meters (kg/m<sup>2</sup>) [<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="B19-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">19</citation>,<citation rid="B20-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="B22-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Adults with a BMI of 25-29.9 kg/m<sup>2</sup> are classified as overweight or pre-obese, while a BMI of 30 kg/m<sup>2</sup> or higher indicates obesity [<citation rid="B19-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">19</citation>], which is further divided into three classes based on severity [<citation rid="B20-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Table 1 summarizes the BMI categories for adults and their corresponding classifications.

Nevertheless, relying exclusively on BMI to diagnose obesity is problematic because it does not differentiate between fat, muscle, and bone mass, nor does it indicate the specific type or location of fat in the body [<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="B23-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S2213-8587(24)00316-4" pmid="39824205" pmcid="PMC11870235" count="1">23</citation>,<citation rid="B24-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12966-025-01719-6" pmid="40001193" pmcid="PMC11863867" count="1">24</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To address this, major health organizations recommend measuring waist circumference to identify visceral fat accumulation, a simple and inexpensive method that strongly predicts metabolic risk. <sentence_start/>Moreover, bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) represents an accessible and non-invasive alternative for estimating body fat percentage and lean mass, offering a practical intermediate option between simple anthropometric measures and advanced imaging techniques. <sentence_start/>For a more precise quantification of body composition, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) can be utilized, though its routine clinical use is limited by cost and availability [<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph21060757" pmid="38929003" pmcid="PMC11204233" count="1">25</citation>].

Recent advancements in the definition of obesity reflect a shift towards evaluating functional health rather than just body size. <sentence_start/>In 2024, the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO) proposed that an individual is considered obese if they have a BMI of 30 or higher, or a BMI of 25 or more, along with a waist-to-height ratio ≥ 0.5, together with obesity-associated health, functional, or psychological conditions [<citation rid="B3-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-024-03095-3" pmid="38969880" count="1">3</citation>].

Furthermore, the Lancet Commission on Clinical Obesity recently proposed a framework distinguishing between “clinical obesity” (excess adiposity causing measurable impairment of organ function or substantially restricting daily functioning, warranting active medical treatment) and “preclinical obesity” (excess body fat without current functional consequences but with elevated risk of progression to clinical obesity and associated NCDs). <sentence_start/>Classification requires confirmation of excess adiposity using BMI combined with at least one body size measurement (waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, or waist-to-height ratio); at least two body size measurements without BMI; or direct body fat quantification by DEXA. <sentence_start/>A BMI above 40 kg/m<sup>2</sup> is considered sufficient on its own. <sentence_start/>This multi-criteria approach addresses the limitations of BMI and better reflects the actual health trajectory of the patient [<citation rid="B23-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S2213-8587(24)00316-4" pmid="39824205" pmcid="PMC11870235" count="1">23</citation>].

The clinical heterogeneity of obesity is further illustrated by the concepts of metabolically healthy obesity (MHO) and metabolically unhealthy obesity (MUO). <sentence_start/>No universally accepted definition of MHO has been established, with most studies classifying individuals as metabolically healthy based on the absence of, or a limited number of, metabolic syndrome components, though criteria may also incorporate markers of insulin resistance or systemic inflammation. <sentence_start/>MHO is generally characterized by preserved insulin sensitivity and predominantly subcutaneous rather than visceral fat accumulation. <sentence_start/>Reported prevalence estimates vary considerably across studies due to inconsistent definitions of metabolic health. <sentence_start/>MHO tends to be more common among women, younger individuals, those with lower BMI (<35 kg/m<sup>2</sup>), and people of European ancestry. <sentence_start/>However, MHO is often a transient state, with a significant proportion of individuals transitioning to MUO over time, underscoring the dynamic and progressive nature of obesity [<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2021.8860" pmid="33961041" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B28-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endrev/bnaa004" pmid="32128581" pmcid="PMC7098708" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="B29-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI129186" pmid="31524630" pmcid="PMC6763224" count="1">29</citation>,<citation rid="B30-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.36011/cpp.2022.4.e19" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="B31-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11154-023-09830-4" pmid="37581871" pmcid="PMC10492670" count="1">31</citation>].
5. <sentence_start/>The Pathophysiology of Obesity

Obesity is a chronic, relapsing, multifactorial disease. <sentence_start/>It results from interactions among genetic susceptibility, neurohormonal and metabolic disturbances, behavioral factors, gut microbiota alterations, aberrant epigenetic modifications, and obesogenic environments characterized by hyperpalatable diets, easy access to high-calorie foods, overindulgence, and sedentary lifestyles. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, obesity extends beyond simple caloric excess or individual behavior, reflecting complex disruptions in the biological systems that regulate energy balance [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mayocp.2023.05.026" pmid="37831039" pmcid="PMC10843116" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B34-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s43556-025-00264-9" pmid="40278960" pmcid="PMC12031720" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Indeed, energy homeostasis depends on hypothalamic and peripheral signals that coordinate intake and expenditure, and even small, sustained positive energy imbalances, potentially as little as 1-2% of daily energy intake, may contribute to substantial long-term weight gain [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B35-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10552-017-0869-z" pmid="28210884" pmcid="PMC5325830" count="1">35</citation>].

At the tissue level, the sustained positive energy balance promotes triglyceride storage in adipocytes distributed across subcutaneous, visceral, pelvic, pericardial, and intramuscular depots. <sentence_start/>White adipose tissue (WAT) primarily stores energy, whereas the mitochondria-rich brown (BAT) and beige (BeAT) adipose tissues support thermogenesis [<citation rid="B34-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s43556-025-00264-9" pmid="40278960" pmcid="PMC12031720" count="1">34</citation>,<citation rid="B36-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2016/6067349" pmid="27073398" pmcid="PMC4814709" count="1">36</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Through uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1)-mediated uncoupled respiration, BAT and BeAT dissipate energy as heat; WAT browning can therefore increase expenditure and limit fat accumulation. <sentence_start/>Conversely, mitochondrial dysfunction and high-fat diets impair thermogenesis, promote insulin resistance, and aggravate metabolic complications [<citation rid="B34-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s43556-025-00264-9" pmid="40278960" pmcid="PMC12031720" count="1">34</citation>].

Beyond its effects on thermogenesis, mitochondrial dysfunction also increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, activating inflammatory pathways that contribute to the chronic low-grade inflammation and insulin resistance associated with obesity [<citation rid="B37-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4093/dmj.2016.40.4.272" pmid="27352152" pmcid="PMC4995181" count="1">37</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.physbeh.2026.115427" pmid="42314854" count="1">38</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition, mutations, deletions, or reduced copy number of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can compromise energy production, increase oxidative stress, and lead to impaired glucose homeostasis, a key feature of obesity-related metabolic dysfunction [<citation rid="B39-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4161/epi.19547" pmid="22419065" pmcid="PMC3368816" count="1">39</citation>,<citation rid="B40-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fcell.2023.1153174" pmid="36968196" pmcid="PMC10036395" count="1">40</citation>].

Peripheral metabolic disturbances also influence neural circuits governing energy homeostasis. <sentence_start/>As a key integrative center, the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) processes hormonal, metabolic, and neural cues to coordinate appetite and energy expenditure. <sentence_start/>Neurons co-expressing neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) are orexigenic; they are stimulated by ghrelin and inhibited by leptin, insulin, amylin, and serotonin. <sentence_start/>AgRP promotes food intake by antagonizing the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R), thereby opposing α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) signaling, reducing satiety, and stimulating overeating. <sentence_start/>Conversely, proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and cocaine- and amphetamine-regulated transcript (CART) neurons suppress appetite and increase energy expenditure. <sentence_start/>POMC-derived α-MSH activates MC4R to promote satiety, while CART also participates in reward-related neural circuits and behavioral responses to psychostimulants such as cocaine and amphetamine. <sentence_start/>In obesity, altered hormonal inputs and central resistance to leptin and insulin disrupt the balance between orexigenic NPY/AgRP and anorexigenic POMC/CART pathways [<citation rid="B41-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">41</citation>].

Peripheral hormones relay nutrient availability and energy stores through the gut-brain axis. <sentence_start/>Ghrelin, secreted by the stomach during fasting periods, stimulates orexigenic neurons in the ARC, thereby promoting food intake, whereas leptin, produced by adipose tissue, engages leptin receptors (LEPR) within the ARC to inhibit hunger and enhance energy expenditure. <sentence_start/>Postprandial enteroendocrine hormones, including cholecystokinin (CCK) and GLP-1, signal to hypothalamic and brainstem circuits through vagal afferent and humoral pathways, promoting satiety and limiting meal size. <sentence_start/>In obesity, impaired leptin transport and signaling, hypothalamic inflammation and cellular stress, altered ghrelin signaling, and reduced responsiveness to satiety hormones, including CCK and GLP-1, sustain hunger and reduce energy expenditure [<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms24043384" pmid="36834794" pmcid="PMC9959457" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B43-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms22126445" pmid="34208585" pmcid="PMC8235268" count="1">43</citation>,<citation rid="B44-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2023.1149239" pmid="37056675" pmcid="PMC10086443" count="1">44</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, excess adiposity, particularly visceral adiposity, together with persistent nutrient excess, impairs insulin signaling in skeletal muscle and liver, reducing glucose utilization and promoting compensatory hyperinsulinemia, hepatic lipogenesis, and continued weight gain [<citation rid="B43-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms22126445" pmid="34208585" pmcid="PMC8235268" count="1">43</citation>,<citation rid="B44-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2023.1149239" pmid="37056675" pmcid="PMC10086443" count="1">44</citation>].
6. <sentence_start/>Limitations of Traditional Nutritional Approaches in Obesity and the Emergence of Precision Nutrition

Traditional nutrition-based strategies for managing obesity typically center on reducing caloric intake and standardized meal plans. <sentence_start/>While these methods can promote initial weight loss, their long-term effectiveness is often limited due to interindividual metabolic differences, physiological adaptations, and difficulties sustaining adherence [<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms252413438" pmid="39769203" pmcid="PMC11676201" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B45-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13679-025-00636-w" pmid="40381089" pmcid="PMC12085324" count="1">45</citation>,<citation rid="B46-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/NU14061259" pmid="35334917" pmcid="PMC8953094" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These limitations are particularly evident with low-energy diets (LEDs) and very-low-energy diets (VLEDs). <sentence_start/>While these regimens can induce rapid weight loss, they may also reduce fat-free mass, which is important for metabolic function and long-term weight control. <sentence_start/>VLEDs may achieve greater initial weight loss, but their long-term outcomes are generally no better than those of less restrictive approaches, and weight is frequently regained once dietary rigidity decreases. <sentence_start/>Highly restrictive regimens, including VLEDs and ketogenic diets, are further limited by inflexibility, potential nutritional insufficiencies, lifestyle barriers, and health risks such as gallstones and endocrine disturbances. <sentence_start/>In contrast, more flexible dietary patterns, such as the Mediterranean diet, tend to support better adherence and more sustainable long-term outcomes [<citation rid="B45-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13679-025-00636-w" pmid="40381089" pmcid="PMC12085324" count="1">45</citation>].

Beyond these practical challenges, the “calories in, calories out” framework provides an incomplete account of weight management. <sentence_start/>It assumes that energy intake and expenditure can be measured precisely and directly linked to changes in body weight. <sentence_start/>However, food labels may substantially misrepresent calorie content, sometimes by up to 60%, making precise energy balance difficult to achieve. <sentence_start/>Moreover, foods with the same energy content may have different metabolic effects: low-glycemic, fiber-rich foods promote satiety and slower glucose absorption, whereas high-glycemic foods can cause rapid insulin rises, favor fat storage, and lead to an earlier return of hunger. <sentence_start/>Thus, food quality influences weight management beyond total caloric intake. <sentence_start/>The framework also fails to fully capture adaptive physiological responses to energy restriction. <sentence_start/>Reduced energy intake can lower basal or resting metabolic rate through adaptive thermogenesis, thereby conserving energy during a perceived deficit. <sentence_start/>Genetic factors, insulin sensitivity, body composition, hormonal profiles, sleep, stress, and activity levels further influence metabolic responses to caloric restriction, limiting the predictive value of a simple caloric model and helping explain why identical dietary interventions may produce different outcomes [<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms252413438" pmid="39769203" pmcid="PMC11676201" count="1">4</citation>].

Consequently, maintaining weight loss remains challenging even after successful short-term dietary interventions, with only around one in four individuals sustaining weight loss over time. <sentence_start/>Long-term maintenance is more likely among those who remain physically active, follow a balanced lower-fat diet, eat breakfast regularly, monitor their weight, and maintain consistent eating routines. <sentence_start/>Environmental management, self-regulation, structured therapeutic strategies, and continued behavioral support are also central to long-term success. <sentence_start/>Self-monitoring tools, including digital applications, can further strengthen adherence and help sustain these behavioral changes during the maintenance phase [<citation rid="B46-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/NU14061259" pmid="35334917" pmcid="PMC8953094" count="1">46</citation>].

Taken together, these limitations emphasize why “one-size-fits-all” dietary approaches are insufficient in the management of obesity. <sentence_start/>Even when individuals follow the same standardized low-calorie, high-protein, or low-carbohydrate diet, they may show markedly different postprandial glucose responses to the same foods, as well as different changes in body composition, metabolic adaptations, and levels of adherence. <sentence_start/>This interindividual variability has driven the emergence of precision nutrition as a more individualized approach to obesity management [<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms252413438" pmid="39769203" pmcid="PMC11676201" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B47-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.advnut.2024.100186" pmid="38316343" pmcid="PMC10914563" count="1">47</citation>].
7. <sentence_start/>Pillars of Individually Tailored Dietary Interventions: The Precision Nutrition Approach

Precision nutrition, also referred to as personalized nutrition, tailors dietary recommendations to individual biological, behavioral, and environmental characteristics, recognizing that responses to the same diet vary and that population-level guidelines may be insufficient for managing and preventing obesity and metabolic diseases. <sentence_start/>To create individualized interventions, precision nutrition integrates diverse factors such as genetic predisposition, physical activity, circadian rhythms, eating behaviors, metabolic status, and gut microbiome composition. <sentence_start/>Omics technologies, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, foodomics, and microbiomics, provide a holistic assessment of biological systems and help identify interindividual differences in nutrient metabolism, food-derived metabolites, and metabotypes associated with metabolic risk. <sentence_start/>Personalized dietary guidance may enhance motivation for behavioral change and lead to superior outcomes in weight management compared with standard, non-personalized approaches [<citation rid="B47-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.advnut.2024.100186" pmid="38316343" pmcid="PMC10914563" count="1">47</citation>,<citation rid="B48-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/NU16050581" pmid="38474710" pmcid="PMC10935146" count="1">48</citation>,<citation rid="B49-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13668-024-00550-y" pmid="38806863" pmcid="PMC11327204" count="1">49</citation>,<citation rid="B50-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13668-023-00491-y" pmid="37610590" pmcid="PMC10766837" count="1">50</citation>].
7.1. <sentence_start/>Genetic Profiling for Dietary Recommendations

Obesity arises from a complex interaction between genetic predisposition and environmental exposures, with research indicating that 40-70% of individual variability in body weight is influenced by hereditary factors. <sentence_start/>From a genetic perspective, obesity can be classified as monogenic or polygenic. <sentence_start/>While the majority of obesity cases are polygenic, rare monogenic forms provide crucial insights into the fundamental biological pathways regulating appetite and energy balance [<citation rid="B49-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13668-024-00550-y" pmid="38806863" pmcid="PMC11327204" count="1">49</citation>,<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu16203562" pmid="39458556" pmcid="PMC11510173" count="1">51</citation>].
7.1.1. <sentence_start/>Monogenic Obesity and Specific Therapies

Monogenic obesity typically affects roughly 1-5% of individuals with severe early-onset obesity and is characterized by hyperphagia and rapid weight gain from early childhood. <sentence_start/>This condition usually results from rare, high-penetrance mutations in single genes that alter the leptin-melanocortin signaling pathway in the hypothalamus. <sentence_start/>The causal role, biological pathway, and molecular function of these genes have already been established through direct biochemical, physiological, and pedigree-based studies, independent of, and prior to, the GWAS that later identified common risk variants with much smaller individual effects. <sentence_start/>Key causal genes include leptin (<italic>LEP</italic>), <italic>LEPR</italic>, <italic>POMC</italic>, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 1 (<italic>PCSK1</italic>), and <italic>MC4R</italic>, each with a well-defined function within the leptin-melanocortin signaling pathway, as summarized in Table 2. <sentence_start/>In addition, obesity is a prominent clinical feature in several pleiotropic genetic syndromes, such as Prader-Willi syndrome and Bardet-Biedl syndrome [<citation rid="B49-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13668-024-00550-y" pmid="38806863" pmcid="PMC11327204" count="1">49</citation>,<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu16203562" pmid="39458556" pmcid="PMC11510173" count="1">51</citation>].

Identifying monogenic obesity is clinically significant because it enables highly targeted, precision pharmacotherapy that addresses the underlying genetic defect, whereas conventional dietary interventions alone yield limited and often insufficient responses in these patients. <sentence_start/>A landmark example of this translational approach is setmelanotide (IMCIVREE<sup>®</sup>), an MC4R agonist approved by the FDA for chronic weight management in patients with specific genetic defects in the leptin-melanocortin pathway. <sentence_start/>Setmelanotide is indicated for individuals with obesity due to POMC, PCSK1, or LEPR deficiency, as well as for patients with Bardet-Biedl syndrome. <sentence_start/>By restoring signaling through the MC4R pathway, this targeted therapy effectively reduces hyperphagia and promotes significant weight loss, representing a paradigm shift toward precision medicine in obesity care [<citation rid="B56-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38301066" count="1">56</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, patients with congenital leptin deficiency due to biallelic <italic>LEP</italic> mutations respond markedly to recombinant human leptin (metreleptin) replacement therapy, which reduces hyperphagia and body weight and improves metabolic parameters, further illustrating the value of genotype-directed treatment in monogenic obesity [<citation rid="B54-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12020-026-04696-3" pmid="42440185" pmcid="PMC13364813" count="1">54</citation>,<citation rid="B57-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/21623945.2025.2508188" pmid="40415699" pmcid="PMC12118419" count="1">57</citation>].
7.1.2. <sentence_start/>Polygenic Obesity

The more prevalent polygenic obesity arises from the combined small effects of numerous common gene variants, distinct from the rare, high-penetrance mutations previously discussed in the case of monogenic obesity. <sentence_start/>In the case of polygenic obesity, behaviors and living conditions, including eating patterns, exercise levels, and psychosocial factors, are key drivers in shaping the expression of genetic vulnerability [<citation rid="B49-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13668-024-00550-y" pmid="38806863" pmcid="PMC11327204" count="1">49</citation>,<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu16203562" pmid="39458556" pmcid="PMC11510173" count="1">51</citation>,<citation rid="B58-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/life15111658" pmid="41302083" pmcid="PMC12653754" count="1">58</citation>,<citation rid="B59-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">59</citation>]. <sentence_start/>GWAS have significantly expanded the understanding of polygenic obesity by identifying numerous loci across the genome that shape energy regulation, food intake behavior, fat accumulation, and variability in weight-loss outcomes. <sentence_start/>Obesity susceptibility is influenced by many genetic variants, particularly single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) [<citation rid="B60-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu16050607" pmid="38474735" pmcid="PMC10934888" count="1">60</citation>,<citation rid="B61-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41366-025-01979-z" pmid="41398384" count="1">61</citation>,<citation rid="B62-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s10038-023-01189-3" pmid="37620670" pmcid="PMC10678330" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Notably, such associations are often population-specific: the rs9939609 variant of the fat mass and obesity-associated gene (<italic>FTO</italic>), robustly linked to obesity in European cohorts, showed no association in a Chinese Han population, underscoring that SNP-based findings should not be generalized across ethnic groups without validation [<citation rid="B63-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2337/db07-1130" pmid="17959933" count="1">63</citation>].

Table 3 summarizes some of the most relevant and well-replicated SNPs statistically associated with susceptibility to obesity in GWAS. <sentence_start/>Unlike the causal monogenic genes described above, whose functional roles were established through direct biochemical and physiological study, the mechanistic annotations below reflect the biological plausibility proposed for each locus and should not be read as proof of a validated causal or functional role. <sentence_start/>The <italic>FTO</italic> gene is known for its influence on appetite and body weight, and variants in <italic>MC4R</italic> are similarly associated with food intake, distinct from the rare loss-of-function <italic>MC4R</italic> mutations that cause monogenic obesity (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Variants in the <italic>LEP</italic> gene are associated with differences in appetite control and metabolic homeostasis. <sentence_start/>Likewise, the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (<italic>PPARG</italic>) gene, important for adipocyte differentiation and fat and glucose metabolism, and the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (<italic>BDNF</italic>) gene, which regulates appetitive behavior and energy balance, harbor common variants associated with obesity risk. <sentence_start/>Similarly, common variants within the apolipoprotein A-II (<italic>APOA2</italic>), fatty acid-binding protein 2 (<italic>FABP2</italic>), and adrenoceptor beta 2 (<italic>ADRB2</italic>) genes, involved, respectively, in gene-diet interactions with saturated fat intake, intestinal dietary fat absorption, and adrenergic-mediated energy expenditure, further help explain the wide range of obesity-related responses among individuals [<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu16203562" pmid="39458556" pmcid="PMC11510173" count="1">51</citation>,<citation rid="B64-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s43042-026-00840-w" count="1">64</citation>,<citation rid="B65-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes14111996" pmid="38002939" pmcid="PMC10671328" count="1">65</citation>,<citation rid="B66-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/genes13060945" pmid="35741707" pmcid="PMC9222344" count="1">66</citation>,<citation rid="B67-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jdiacomp.2025.109209" pmid="41264996" count="1">67</citation>,<citation rid="B68-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pnpbp.2025.111457" pmid="40701213" count="1">68</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fgene.2026.1784283" pmid="42039698" pmcid="PMC13105473" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="B70-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/ajcn/nqy081" pmid="29901700" pmcid="PMC6454512" count="1">70</citation>].

The integration of genome-wide SNP data into personalized dietary recommendations represents an emerging strategy in the management of obesity [<citation rid="B82-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu16162673" pmid="39203810" pmcid="PMC11357412" count="1">82</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Some large-scale trials have reported encouraging results in this direction. <sentence_start/>In the multinational Food4Me trial, participants informed of their <italic>FTO</italic> obesity-risk-allele status as part of a genetically personalized intervention showed significantly greater reductions in body weight and waist circumference than non-risk-allele carriers within the same intervention arm [<citation rid="B83-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3945/ajcn.116.145680" pmid="28381478" count="1">83</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Likewise, in the NOW trial, incorporating nutrigenomics-based guidance into a structured lifestyle program yielded significantly greater short- and medium-term reductions in body fat percentage than the standard program alone [<citation rid="B84-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/oby.22880" pmid="32935529" count="1">84</citation>].

Nevertheless, other studies specifically testing whether matching diet composition to genotype, rather than simply disclosing genetic risk or adding nutrigenomic guidance to standard counseling, outperforms standard advice have shown more limited clinical evidence. <sentence_start/>For instance, the Personalized Nutrition Study (POINTS) study classified 145 adults with overweight or obesity as fat- or carbohydrate-responders based on ten SNPs and randomized them to a high-fat or high-carbohydrate diet, resulting in genotype-concordant and genotype-discordant subgroups. <sentence_start/>There was no significant difference in weight loss between these subgroups (−5.3 kg vs. −4.8 kg) after 12 weeks [<citation rid="B85-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-41969-1" pmid="37813841" pmcid="PMC10562431" count="1">85</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Likewise, the MyGeneMyDiet study compared genotype-informed lifestyle recommendations against standard dietary advice in Filipino adults with overweight and obesity over 12 months, and found no evidence of meaningful between-group differences in weight, BMI, waist circumference, body fat percentage, or metabolic markers at any timepoint, although the small final sample size (27 completers out of 52 who initiated the intervention) may limit the strength of these results [<citation rid="B86-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12263-026-00794-z" pmid="41654718" pmcid="PMC12977431" count="1">86</citation>].

These findings are consistent with a broader pattern in the literature: while the theoretical framework for genotype-guided dietary intervention is well-established, the translation of SNPs data into clinically meaningful and superior outcomes over standard advice remains largely unproven for approaches specifically matching diet type to genotype. <sentence_start/>It is also important not to conflate statistical association with functional validation: a GWAS hit indicates that a locus is statistically linked to obesity risk in a given population, not that the underlying variant has been experimentally shown to cause the phenotype through the proposed mechanism. <sentence_start/>Several factors contribute to the limited clinical translation of these findings. <sentence_start/>First, individual SNPs and even multi-SNP genetic risk scores typically explain only a modest fraction of the variance in BMI and adiposity, an effect size consistent with the minimal, largely non-actionable contribution of any single common variant, given that obesity is a highly polygenic and environmentally modulated trait. <sentence_start/>Second, current SNP panels do not yet capture the full complexity of nutrient metabolism, which is further shaped by aberrant epigenetic modifications, the gut microbiome, metabolic phenotype, and behavioral factors that static genomic data alone cannot reflect. <sentence_start/>Therefore, progress in the field will require the integration of multi-omics approaches, larger GWAS datasets, and rigorously designed randomized controlled trials before genotype-guided nutrition can be implemented as a standard clinical tool in obesity [<citation rid="B49-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13668-024-00550-y" pmid="38806863" pmcid="PMC11327204" count="1">49</citation>,<citation rid="B86-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12263-026-00794-z" pmid="41654718" pmcid="PMC12977431" count="1">86</citation>,<citation rid="B87-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/obr.13941" pmid="40375759" pmcid="PMC12318916" count="1">87</citation>].

One such underexplored multi-omics direction involves tracing genetic variation back to the enzymatic steps of carbohydrate, protein, and lipid metabolism themselves, rather than stopping at associations between SNPs and downstream phenotypes such as body weight. <sentence_start/>SNPs affecting the activity of specific metabolic enzymes may offer greater explanatory value for individual dietary responses than SNPs associated only with such distal phenotypic effects. <sentence_start/>The mitochondrial dysfunction, discussed in Section 5, can be understood in this context as a downstream signal of upstream disruptions in these biochemical pathways rather than a primary cause in itself. <sentence_start/>For instance, excess branched-chain amino acid availability, reflecting altered protein catabolism, has been shown to suppress mitochondrial function and biogenic signaling in a skeletal muscle model of insulin resistance, illustrating how a specific macronutrient-metabolizing pathway can drive mitochondrial impairment [<citation rid="B88-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/metabo14070389" pmid="39057712" pmcid="PMC11279211" count="1">88</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Greater attention to causal genes involved in macronutrient metabolism may therefore complement current SNP-based approaches to precision nutrition.
7.2. <sentence_start/>Metabolomic-Guided Dietary Adjustments

Metabolomics, one of the major omics disciplines, analyzes low-molecular-weight metabolites that represent intermediate or final products of biochemical pathways at cellular and systemic levels. <sentence_start/>By integrating both intrinsic host processes and influences from digestion, nutrient metabolism, and gut microbiota activity, the metabolomic profile provides a broad overview of an individual’s overall physiological state. <sentence_start/>In obesity, it can reveal molecular alterations associated with excess adiposity and identify biomarkers of metabolic dysregulation, including impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance [<citation rid="B89-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18549/PharmPract.2026.1.3428" count="1">89</citation>,<citation rid="B90-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.arcmed.2023.02.007" pmid="36990891" count="1">90</citation>].

A compelling illustration of metabolomics applied in interventions to combat obesity is provided by the POUNDS Lost trial, a 2-year randomized controlled trial in 811 adults with overweight or obesity assigned to four diets varying in protein and fat content. <sentence_start/>Metabolomic analyses within this trial revealed that reductions in circulating branched-chain amino acids (valine, leucine, isoleucine) and aromatic amino acids during the intervention were significantly associated with improvements in insulin resistance and reductions in triglycerides, independent of the amount of weight lost. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that metabolomic profiling can identify metabolic responders to dietary intervention beyond what anthropometric measures alone can capture, supporting the use of metabolomics to monitor and guide precision dietary strategies in obesity management [<citation rid="B91-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15163665" pmid="37630855" pmcid="PMC10458797" count="1">91</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, the following subsections examine two complementary dimensions of this metabolic heterogeneity: personalized glycemic responses and lipidomic alterations related to fatty acid metabolism.
7.2.1. <sentence_start/>Personalized Glycemic Response

Personalized glycemic response describes the substantial interindividual variability in postprandial glycemic responses (PPGRs) after identical meals, challenging the assumption that foods exert uniform glycemic effects based on carbohydrate content or glycemic index alone. <sentence_start/>Frequent postprandial glucose (PPG) elevations are associated with altered glucose homeostasis, hyperinsulinemia, and obesity-related metabolic dysfunction [<citation rid="B92-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-025-03719-2" pmid="40467897" pmcid="PMC12283382" count="1">92</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Elevated PPG stimulates insulin secretion and may promote weight gain, whereas well-regulated PPG may preserve insulin sensitivity, improve satiety, and support weight loss. <sentence_start/>Given the considerable variability in these responses among individuals, standardized nutritional guidelines may not adequately reflect personal metabolic needs [<citation rid="B93-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nut.2024.112641" pmid="39705786" count="1">93</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This concept is most directly actionable for individuals with, or at high risk of, dysglycemia and type 2 diabetes mellitus. <sentence_start/>Therefore, glycemia-guided personalization should be regarded as one tool within a broader personalization strategy rather than a universal requirement of obesity care [<citation rid="B94-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/dmso.s528619" pmid="40821750" pmcid="PMC12350580" count="1">94</citation>].

A first source of variability in PPGRs lies in meal composition and sequencing rather than carbohydrate content alone. <sentence_start/>In a controlled trial of standardized carbohydrate meals (rice, bread, potatoes, pasta, beans, grapes, and mixed berries) with equivalent glycemic loads, postprandial responses varied substantially between individuals, and consuming small amounts of fiber, protein, or fat before carbohydrate intake modestly blunted glycemic peaks in many participants, underscoring the role of nutrient composition and food characteristics in modulating glycemic response beyond carbohydrate quantity alone. <sentence_start/>A second, individual-level source is the person’s own metabolic phenotype: within the same trial, participants with greater insulin resistance or pancreatic β-cell dysfunction showed higher glucose responses to starch-rich foods such as potatoes and pasta, and the benefit of meal sequencing was blunted in these individuals, indicating that food-based strategies interact with, rather than override, the underlying metabolic phenotype [<citation rid="B92-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-025-03719-2" pmid="40467897" pmcid="PMC12283382" count="1">92</citation>].

A third factor contributing to variability in glycemic responses is the gut microbiota. <sentence_start/>Gut microbial composition and functional activity may influence carbohydrate metabolism and PPGRs via fermentation metabolites, inflammatory pathways, and insulin signaling. <sentence_start/>Thus, incorporating microbiota features into predictive models may improve glycemic response estimation beyond conventional dietary approaches [<citation rid="B90-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.arcmed.2023.02.007" pmid="36990891" count="1">90</citation>].

Clinical evidence increasingly supports the value of glycemia-guided personalization: continuous glucose monitoring-guided nutrition counseling produced significantly greater reductions in body weight, BMI, body fat mass and waist-to-hip ratio than conventional advice over 12 weeks in adults with obesity [<citation rid="B93-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.nut.2024.112641" pmid="39705786" count="1">93</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Likewise, Zeevi et al. developed and validated a ML algorithm integrating diet, physical activity, anthropometrics, blood parameters, and gut microbiota composition to predict PPGRs, and showed in a small randomized trial that algorithm-guided diets reduced glucose spikes alongside favorable microbiota shifts [<citation rid="B95-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2015.11.001" pmid="26590418" count="1">95</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Applying the Zeevi et al. algorithm [<citation rid="B95-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2015.11.001" pmid="26590418" count="1">95</citation>], the Personal Diet Study found comparable six-month weight loss (approximately 3-4%) between a standardized low-fat diet and the algorithm-guided intervention in adults with obesity and impaired glucose metabolism, although individual responses varied considerably, suggesting some individuals may derive greater benefit from personalized strategies than others [<citation rid="B96-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2022.33760" pmid="36169954" pmcid="PMC9520362" count="1">96</citation>].

More recently, the ZOE METHOD trial compared, among 347 US adults, an 18-week app-based personalized dietary program, based on food characteristics, individual postprandial glucose and triglyceride responses, gut microbiome composition, and health history, against standard US Department of Agriculture-based dietary advice, and found significantly greater reductions in triglycerides, along with secondary improvements in body weight, waist circumference, and microbiome diversity, particularly among highly adherent participants. <sentence_start/>However, as this trial was conducted in a generally healthy population rather than an obesity-specific cohort, its findings should not be over-generalized to individuals with obesity [<citation rid="B97-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-024-02951-6" pmid="38714898" pmcid="PMC11271409" count="1">97</citation>].

Taken together, glycemic responses to food reflect an interplay of meal composition, individual metabolic phenotype, and gut microbial characteristics, and predictive tools accounting for this complexity may improve the personalization of dietary strategies for obesity management. <sentence_start/>Although current evidence is encouraging, further long-term trials are needed to clarify which individuals benefit most from personalized glycemic interventions and whether these approaches translate into clinically meaningful, sustained weight loss.
7.2.2. <sentence_start/>Lipidomics and Fatty Acid Metabolism

Lipidomics may provide a more detailed assessment of obesity-related cardiometabolic dysfunction than conventional lipid panels by characterizing individual lipid species and metabolic pathways [<citation rid="B98-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2019/1382418" pmid="31915678" pmcid="PMC6930386" count="1">98</citation>,<citation rid="B99-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/diagnostics13040721" pmid="36832218" pmcid="PMC9954993" count="1">99</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Obesity-associated lipidomic profiles commonly show increased saturated lipid metabolites, reduced unsaturated fatty acids, particularly polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), and altered phospholipid metabolism, changes associated with insulin resistance, visceral adiposity, hypertriglyceridemia, and persistent low-grade inflammation [<citation rid="B100-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-023-38703-8" pmid="37474543" pmcid="PMC10359283" count="1">100</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Reduced lysophosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylcholine species may reflect disturbances in choline-dependent one-carbon metabolism, epigenetic regulation, and energy homeostasis, while enzymes such as PHOSPHO1 connect phospholipid turnover with insulin sensitivity and adipose-tissue thermogenesis [<citation rid="B101-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2022.935195" pmid="35957983" pmcid="PMC9360546" count="1">101</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As some abnormalities may precede overt obesity or conventional dyslipidemia, lipidomic biomarkers may support early risk assessment and personalized nutrition [<citation rid="B98-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2019/1382418" pmid="31915678" pmcid="PMC6930386" count="1">98</citation>].

Furthermore, fatty acid composition and metabolism are central to obesity-related metabolic dysfunction. <sentence_start/>Saturated fatty acids (SFAs), especially palmitic acid, promote inflammation, impaired insulin signaling, hepatic steatosis, and lipotoxicity. <sentence_start/>Likewise, combined high intakes of SFAs and simple carbohydrates can increase ceramide synthesis, which is linked to insulin resistance, mitochondrial dysfunction, and metabolic inflammation. <sentence_start/>The broader relevance of this pathway is reflected in its involvement in sphingolipid lysosomal storage disorders [<citation rid="B102-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12944-021-01466-0" pmid="33941173" pmcid="PMC8094529" count="1">102</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast, monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) and PUFAs are generally associated with improved membrane function, enhanced insulin sensitivity, and more efficient fatty acid oxidation, via carnitine shuttle-dependent mitochondrial and peroxisomal pathways; dietary fatty acid composition itself directly regulates mitochondrial structure and function, indicating that the metabolic impact of dietary fat depends on fatty acid composition and its subsequent oxidative processing, and not simply on total fat intake [<citation rid="B103-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.clnesp.2025.11.156" pmid="41344402" count="1">103</citation>,<citation rid="B104-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11154-018-9448-1" pmid="29926323" pmcid="PMC6208583" count="1">104</citation>,<citation rid="B105-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/advances/nmy007" pmid="29767698" pmcid="PMC5952932" count="1">105</citation>].

Numerous dietary intervention studies have demonstrated that modifying the type of fat consumed favorably influences lipidomic profiles and metabolic outcomes in obesity. <sentence_start/>Diets rich in oleic acid, the main MUFA in olive oil, reduce ceramide concentrations and enhance insulin sensitivity compared with diets high in palmitic acid and other SFAs. <sentence_start/>Likewise, overfeeding studies show that saturated fat-rich diets promote ceramide accumulation and liver fat, whereas PUFA-enriched diets preserve a more favorable lipid profile despite similar weight gain. <sentence_start/>Foods naturally rich in unsaturated fatty acids, including extra virgin olive oil, fatty fish, and walnuts, may similarly lower circulating ceramides and other lipid intermediates involved in inflammation and insulin resistance [<citation rid="B103-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.clnesp.2025.11.156" pmid="41344402" count="1">103</citation>,<citation rid="B106-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.clnu.2023.06.027" pmid="37421852" count="1">106</citation>,<citation rid="B107-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dmrr.3492" pmid="34435429" pmcid="PMC9286378" count="1">107</citation>,<citation rid="B108-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-024-03124-1" pmid="38992128" pmcid="PMC11485259" count="1">108</citation>,<citation rid="B109-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajcnut.2023.03.024" pmid="37062359" pmcid="PMC10315407" count="1">109</citation>].

Omega-3 PUFAs, particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), may stimulate fat oxidation, support mitochondrial function, improve insulin sensitivity, while reducing hepatic lipid accumulation and pro-inflammatory mediator production. <sentence_start/>Conversely, a high omega-6-to-omega-3 ratio may promote metabolic dysregulation, making this dietary balance relevant to metabolic health in obesity [<citation rid="B110-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu12092751" pmid="32927614" pmcid="PMC7551151" count="1">110</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Finally, genetic factors and variation in fatty acid-metabolizing enzymes may influence PUFAs metabolism, insulin sensitivity, inflammatory status, and lipid profiles. <sentence_start/>Lipidomic profiling may therefore identify metabolic phenotypes and guide individualized interventions, including targeted omega-3 supplementation and personalized modifications in fat intake [<citation rid="B111-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/metabo15090595" pmid="41002979" pmcid="PMC12472015" count="1">111</citation>].
7.3. <sentence_start/>Microbiome-Targeted Interventions

<italic>Bacillota</italic> (formerly <italic>Firmicutes</italic>) and <italic>Bacteroidota</italic> (formerly <italic>Bacteroidetes</italic>) are the dominant phyla in the gut microbiota, while <italic>Pseudomonadota</italic> (formerly <italic>Proteobacteria</italic>), <italic>Verrucomicrobiota</italic> (formerly <italic>Verrucomicrobia</italic>), and <italic>Actinomycetota</italic> (formerly <italic>Actinobacteria</italic>) are found in smaller amounts, together contributing to nutrient assimilation, immune regulation, and host metabolic functions. <sentence_start/>Obesity is frequently associated with reduced microbial diversity and an increased <italic>Bacillota</italic> to <italic>Bacteroidota</italic> ratio, although this finding remains inconsistent [<citation rid="B112-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu14010012" pmid="35010887" pmcid="PMC8746372" count="1">112</citation>,<citation rid="B113-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.dsx.2025.103208" pmid="39999537" count="1">113</citation>,<citation rid="B114-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/amh70010005" count="1">114</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Independently of this ratio, obesity-associated dysbiosis has been linked to reduced abundance of taxa such as <italic>Akkermansia muciniphila</italic> and <italic>Faecalibacterium prausnitzii</italic>, along with functional shifts in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, bile acid signaling, and intestinal barrier integrity, which may contribute to impaired glucose regulation and persistent low-grade inflammation [<citation rid="B115-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/biomedicines13092173" pmid="41007736" pmcid="PMC12467942" count="1">115</citation>,<citation rid="B116-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41579-020-0433-9" pmid="32887946" count="1">116</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Obesity-associated dysbiosis has also been linked to decreased intestinal expression of fasting-induced adipose factor (Fiaf) and impaired signaling of anorexigenic gut hormones like GLP-1 and peptide YY (PYY), which may promote energy intake and lipid storage [<citation rid="B117-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu13103627" pmid="34684633" pmcid="PMC8540110" count="1">117</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings have prompted interest in probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation to modulate the gut microbiota in obesity management [<citation rid="B118-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms26136282" pmid="40650060" pmcid="PMC12249903" count="1">118</citation>].
7.3.1. <sentence_start/>Probiotics and Prebiotics

Probiotics are viable microorganisms that confer health benefits when ingested in adequate amounts. <sentence_start/>Strains of <italic>Lactobacillus</italic> and <italic>Bifidobacterium</italic> may influence body weight through production of SCFA from fiber fermentation, upregulation of satiety hormones (GLP-1, PYY, CCK, leptin), suppression of the “hunger hormone” ghrelin, gut-brain signaling, and restoration of gut barrier integrity. <sentence_start/>Evidence is strongest for SCFAs-mediated stimulation of GLP-1 and PYY, while overall efficacy depends on strain, dosage, duration of supplementation, and host characteristics [<citation rid="B114-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/amh70010005" count="1">114</citation>,<citation rid="B118-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms26136282" pmid="40650060" pmcid="PMC12249903" count="1">118</citation>,<citation rid="B119-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7759/cureus.40948" pmid="37503494" pmcid="PMC10368799" count="1">119</citation>,<citation rid="B120-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12602-024-10363-8" pmid="39320636" count="1">120</citation>].

Clinical evidence supports modest but meaningful benefits of probiotic supplementation in obesity management. <sentence_start/><italic>Lactobacillus gasseri</italic> SBT2055, one of the most studied strains, reduced body weight, BMI, waist circumference, and visceral fat when consumed as fermented milk or yoghurt (100-200 g/day) for 12 weeks compared to placebo. <sentence_start/>Similar outcomes have been reported for other <italic>Lactobacillus</italic> and <italic>Bifidobacterium</italic> strains over 6-12 week interventions, whereas shorter trials of 3-4 weeks were generally ineffective [<citation rid="B114-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/amh70010005" count="1">114</citation>,<citation rid="B117-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu13103627" pmid="34684633" pmcid="PMC8540110" count="1">117</citation>,<citation rid="B121-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202300864RR" pmid="37843880" count="1">121</citation>,<citation rid="B122-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/osp4.759" pmid="38903852" pmcid="PMC11187407" count="1">122</citation>,<citation rid="B123-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/microorganisms8081148" pmid="32751306" pmcid="PMC7465252" count="1">123</citation>].

Multi-strain probiotic formulations may yield more consistent results. <sentence_start/>A six-month RCT using a five-strain combination (<italic>L. acidophilus</italic> CUL60, CUL21; <italic>L. plantarum</italic> CUL66; <italic>B. bifidum</italic> CUL20; <italic>B. animalis</italic> subsp. <italic>lactis</italic> CUL34; 5 × 10<sup>10</sup> CFU/capsule) achieved a mean weight reduction of ~1.3 kg with improvements in BMI and body composition [<citation rid="B124-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-020-60991-7" pmid="32144319" pmcid="PMC7060206" count="1">124</citation>], consistent with meta-analytic estimates of modest reductions in body weight (~0.5-0.6 kg), BMI (~0.3 kg/m<sup>2</sup>), and fat mass, more pronounced beyond eight weeks and when combined with caloric restriction or exercise [<citation rid="B120-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12602-024-10363-8" pmid="39320636" count="1">120</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Notably, while strains such as <italic>L. gasseri</italic> SBT2055 promote weight loss, others such as certain <italic>L. acidophilus</italic> strains may paradoxically increase weight by altering carbohydrate metabolism, underscoring the need for individualized strain selection [<citation rid="B114-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/amh70010005" count="1">114</citation>].

Prebiotics, including inulin, fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS), and galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS), are indigestible dietary compounds that selectively stimulate beneficial gut bacteria. <sentence_start/>In obesity management, their fermentation into SCFAs may enhance satiety by stimulating PYY and GLP-1 secretion and potentially reducing circulating ghrelin. <sentence_start/>SCFAs also support intestinal barrier integrity and may attenuate metabolic endotoxemia and the chronic low-grade inflammation characteristic of metabolic syndrome [<citation rid="B113-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.dsx.2025.103208" pmid="39999537" count="1">113</citation>,<citation rid="B119-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7759/cureus.40948" pmid="37503494" pmcid="PMC10368799" count="1">119</citation>,<citation rid="B125-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcla.24420" pmid="35421277" pmcid="PMC9102524" count="1">125</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, prebiotic efficacy varies according to baseline gut microbiota composition. <sentence_start/>Inulin-type fructans, for instance, show heterogeneous metabolic effects depending on the pre-existing microbial ecosystem, making standardized protocols difficult to establish. <sentence_start/>Metagenomic profiling may therefore enable the development of targeted fiber formulations tailored to individual gut ecology, supporting precision nutrition approaches [<citation rid="B126-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2022.1025706" pmid="36339448" pmcid="PMC9630587" count="1">126</citation>,<citation rid="B127-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms25094834" pmid="38732060" pmcid="PMC11084426" count="1">127</citation>,<citation rid="B128-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41366-024-01590-8" pmid="39033197" pmcid="PMC11584386" count="1">128</citation>,<citation rid="B129-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41392-021-00758-2" pmid="34625537" pmcid="PMC8501008" count="1">129</citation>].
7.3.2. <sentence_start/>Fecal Microbiota Transplantation

Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) involves transferring gut microorganisms from a healthy donor to a recipient, typically via duodenal endoscopy or colonoscopy, to restore microbial diversity and metabolic homeostasis [<citation rid="B125-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcla.24420" pmid="35421277" pmcid="PMC9102524" count="1">125</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Clinical studies indicate that FMT from lean donors may improve gut barrier function, insulin sensitivity, metabolic parameters, and bile acid metabolism in individuals with obesity, partly through increased abundance of <italic>Faecalibacterium</italic> species [<citation rid="B130-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7759/cureus.76858" pmid="39901991" pmcid="PMC11788455" count="1">130</citation>,<citation rid="B131-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.12998/wjcc.v11.i19.4612" pmid="37469721" pmcid="PMC10353513" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although its effects on BMI are generally limited, a four-year follow-up study in adolescents showed sustained reductions in waist circumference, body fat, and systemic inflammation, alongside increased HDL-cholesterol and persistent microbiome changes [<citation rid="B132-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-62752-4" pmid="40877311" pmcid="PMC12394558" count="1">132</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, efficacy varies with donor microbial profile, recipient characteristics, and treatment protocols. <sentence_start/>Overall, FMT appears more promising as a complementary strategy for improving metabolic health and inflammation than as a primary weight loss intervention [<citation rid="B130-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7759/cureus.76858" pmid="39901991" pmcid="PMC11788455" count="1">130</citation>].
7.4. <sentence_start/>Chrono-Nutrition: Timing of Food Intake as a Personalization Target

Beyond the quantity and quality of the diet, growing evidence indicates that the timing of food intake independently influences body weight and metabolic health, giving rise to the field of chrono-nutrition. <sentence_start/>Time-restricted eating (TRE), which confines daily food intake to a fixed window without necessarily prescribing caloric restriction, has been the most extensively studied approach in this context. <sentence_start/>In a landmark trial, a 10 h TRE window reduced body weight, blood pressure, and atherogenic lipids in adults with metabolic syndrome. <sentence_start/>A systematic review and meta-analysis focusing specifically on adults with obesity similarly found that TRE produced reductions in body weight and fat mass. <sentence_start/>More broadly, a recent network meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials comparing multiple intermittent fasting strategies confirmed clinically meaningful reductions in body weight and several cardiometabolic risk factors, although effects were generally comparable to those achieved with continuous caloric restriction, suggesting that part of the benefit may stem from spontaneous reductions in energy intake rather than meal timing per se [<citation rid="B133-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnut.2023.1079250" pmid="36875837" pmcid="PMC9979543" count="1">133</citation>,<citation rid="B134-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cmet.2019.11.004" pmid="31813824" pmcid="PMC6953486" count="1">134</citation>,<citation rid="B135-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj-2024-082007" pmid="40533200" pmcid="PMC12175170" count="1">135</citation>].

A key limitation of current chrono-nutrition research is that most intervention protocols apply a fixed eating window uniformly across participants, without accounting for individual circadian biology. <sentence_start/>Chronotype, the behavioral manifestation of an individual’s intrinsic circadian phase, is influenced by genetic variation in core clock genes and determines each person’s natural propensity toward morningness or eveningness. <sentence_start/>This, in turn, influences appetite regulation, glucose tolerance, and the metabolic response to meal timing throughout the day. <sentence_start/>Individuals with an evening chronotype, for instance, tend to exhibit poorer glycemic control and greater difficulty adhering to early time-restricted eating protocols than those with a morning chronotype. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that aligning the timing of food intake with an individual’s chronotype, rather than applying a standardized eating window, may represent an underexplored but promising dimension of precision nutrition, warranting integration alongside genetic, metabolomic, and microbiome profiling as part of a comprehensive personalization strategy [<citation rid="B136-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2022.1008820" pmid="36479212" pmcid="PMC9720311" count="1">136</citation>,<citation rid="B137-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms24032571" pmid="36768893" pmcid="PMC9916946" count="1">137</citation>].
7.5. <sentence_start/>Behavioral and Lifestyle Integration
