Behavioral and lifestyle factors constitute essential components of precision nutrition, as the long-term success of obesity management depends not only on an individual’s biological characteristics but also on their ability to adopt and sustain meaningful changes in everyday habits. <sentence_start/>Personalized dietary interventions are therefore more likely to be effective when they are aligned with personal food preferences, cultural practices, psychosocial circumstances, and daily routines, including physical activity patterns, sleep habits, and stress management [<citation rid="B47-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.advnut.2024.100186" pmid="38316343" pmcid="PMC10914563" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Psychological characteristics such as motivation, self-efficacy, and self-regulation further influence the capacity to maintain these changes over time [<citation rid="B138-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7196/SAMJ.2025.v115i9b.3698" pmid="41378656" count="1">138</citation>].

A wide range of behavioral techniques has been shown to support adherence to personalized interventions. <sentence_start/>Common behavioral strategies include monitoring dietary intake, physical activity, and body weight to improve self-awareness and support ongoing commitment to healthier behaviors, together with setting achievable goals that promote long-term change. <sentence_start/>Additional strategies involve problem-solving techniques designed to help individuals overcome obstacles that may interfere, stress management to reduce emotionally driven eating, and stimulus control, which focuses on modifying environmental factors that encourage overeating or sedentary behavior. <sentence_start/>Support from family, friends, and healthcare professionals has also been associated with improved weight-loss maintenance [<citation rid="B139-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7759/cureus.18080" pmid="34671541" pmcid="PMC8522530" count="1">139</citation>].

Recent evidence has further emphasized the importance of addressing the psychological mechanisms underlying eating behavior. <sentence_start/>Food cravings are influenced by neurobiological reward pathways and conditioned responses to highly palatable foods, which may trigger eating in the absence of physiological hunger. <sentence_start/>Educating individuals about these processes can reduce self-blame and facilitate the development of more effective coping strategies. <sentence_start/>Approaches grounded in acceptance and commitment may provide additional benefit by strengthening the ability to tolerate discomfort, manage cravings, and maintain behaviors that are consistent with personal values and long-term health goals [<citation rid="B138-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7196/SAMJ.2025.v115i9b.3698" pmid="41378656" count="1">138</citation>].

Lifestyle-related factors are equally important for achieving and preserving weight loss. <sentence_start/>Adequate and consistent sleep has been associated with improved appetite regulation and a lower likelihood of weight regain, whereas regular physical activity contributes to weight maintenance, preservation of lean body mass, and improvements in both metabolic and psychological health. <sentence_start/>Comprehensive interventions generally recommend at least 150 min per week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise during the initial phase of weight loss, with higher levels of physical activity, approximately 200 to 300 min per week, often suggested to support long-term weight maintenance. <sentence_start/>Reducing sedentary time and incorporating movement into daily routines may further enhance the sustainability of personalized obesity treatment strategies [<citation rid="B140-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1037/amp0000517" pmid="32052997" pmcid="PMC7027681" count="1">140</citation>,<citation rid="B141-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu18010012" pmid="41515130" pmcid="PMC12787890" count="1">141</citation>].
7.6. <sentence_start/>Enhancing GLP-1 Efficacy with Personalized Nutrition
7.6.1. <sentence_start/>GLP-1 and Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Obesity Management

Currently available pharmacological therapies for the management of obesity include several agents that act through distinct mechanisms. <sentence_start/>Orlistat is a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor that reduces dietary fat absorption, but its use is often limited by gastrointestinal adverse effects, including oily fecal spotting and urgency in more than 25% of patients, along with decreased absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. <sentence_start/>Phentermine-topiramate and naltrexone-bupropion act on the central nervous system to suppress appetite but are constrained by neuropsychiatric and cardiovascular effects, including insomnia, paresthesia, and teratogenicity with topiramate, and contraindication in seizure disorders and uncontrolled hypertension with naltrexone-bupropion [<citation rid="B142-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jama.2024.10816" pmid="39037780" count="1">142</citation>].

More recently, obesity therapies targeting gut-derived hormones have emerged, producing substantially greater weight loss in head-to-head comparisons against placebo (semaglutide, 11.4%; tirzepatide, 12.4%) than orlistat (3.1%), naltrexone-bupropion (4.1%), or phentermine-topiramate (8.0%), while also demonstrating a broader range of systemic benefits, including glucometabolic, cardiovascular, hepatic, and renal effects, in dedicated outcome trials. <sentence_start/>This combination of superior efficacy and pleiotropic health benefits has positioned gut hormone-based drugs, modeled on hormones known as incretins, as the current cornerstone of obesity pharmacotherapy [<citation rid="B142-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jama.2024.10816" pmid="39037780" count="1">142</citation>,<citation rid="B143-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s44324-024-00030-5" pmid="40604322" pmcid="PMC12118674" count="1">143</citation>].

Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and GLP-1 are the two primary incretin hormones in humans. <sentence_start/>GIP is secreted by K-cells, predominantly located in the duodenum and jejunum, whereas GLP-1 is secreted by L-cells, which are distributed mainly in the ileum and colon. <sentence_start/>L-cells also co-secrete PYY hormone, which reduces appetite and regulates glucose metabolism [<citation rid="B144-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2026.1784709" pmid="41788781" pmcid="PMC12956794" count="1">144</citation>,<citation rid="B145-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms27010027" pmid="41515907" pmcid="PMC12785922" count="1">145</citation>].

Together, GIP and GLP-1 mediate the incretin effect, a physiological phenomenon characterized by enhanced insulin secretion following oral glucose administration compared with an identical glucose load delivered intravenously, reflecting their central role in postprandial glycemic control. <sentence_start/>GIP and GLP-1 receptors are expressed in pancreatic, neural, gastrointestinal, adipose, and other metabolically relevant tissues, enabling effects beyond insulin secretion. <sentence_start/>GLP-1 inhibits glucagon secretion during hyperglycemia and euglycemia, but not during hypoglycemia, delays gastric emptying, and promotes satiety via central nervous system circuits. <sentence_start/>GIP, by contrast, has little effect on glucagon during hyperglycemia but promotes glucagon secretion under fasting, euglycemic, and hypoglycemic conditions. <sentence_start/>In adipose tissue, GIP facilitates postprandial lipid uptake and storage, partly by enhancing insulin-dependent lipoprotein lipase activity. <sentence_start/>Its role in appetite control has historically been considered modest relative to GLP-1, though preclinical evidence suggests central GIP receptor signaling may contribute to reductions in food intake [<citation rid="B145-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms27010027" pmid="41515907" pmcid="PMC12785922" count="1">145</citation>,<citation rid="B146-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2024.1431292" pmid="39114288" pmcid="PMC11304055" count="1">146</citation>].

These physiological actions of endogenous incretin hormones have been pharmacologically leveraged in the development of GLP-1 receptor agonists (RAs) (e.g., semaglutide, liraglutide), as well as newer dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs, including tirzepatide [<citation rid="B147-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/obesities5040088" count="1">147</citation>,<citation rid="B148-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-026-04397-4" pmid="42120724" count="1">148</citation>,<citation rid="B149-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41573-026-01427-1" pmid="42129460" count="1">149</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Building on this progression, triple-hormone agonists represent the next stage in incretin-based drug development. <sentence_start/>For instance, retatrutide, an investigational first-in-class triple GIP/GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist, has recently demonstrated topline weight-loss results in the Phase 3 TRIUMPH-1 trial, with 45.3% of participants on the 12 mg dose achieving ≥30% weight loss at 80 weeks, a magnitude previously associated only with bariatric surgery. <sentence_start/>This positions retatrutide as a potentially transformative pharmacological option for obesity management, pending full peer-reviewed data and regulatory approval [<citation rid="B150-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/08998280.2025.2456441" pmid="40291085" pmcid="PMC12026077" count="1">150</citation>,<citation rid="B151-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" count="1">151</citation>].

GLP-1 RAs and dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs are generally prescribed alongside lifestyle modification in individuals with a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m<sup>2</sup> or a BMI ≥ 27 kg/m<sup>2</sup> accompanied by at least one obesity-related comorbidity [<citation rid="B152-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/oby.24067" pmid="38853526" count="1">152</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Beyond weight loss, emerging evidence suggests that these therapies provide beneficial effects across several obesity-associated comorbidities, including cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and certain types of cancer [<citation rid="B147-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/obesities5040088" count="1">147</citation>,<citation rid="B153-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2307563" pmid="37952131" count="1">153</citation>,<citation rid="B154-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-024-03015-5" pmid="38796653" pmcid="PMC11271413" count="1">154</citation>,<citation rid="B155-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.japhar.2026.100032" count="1">155</citation>,<citation rid="B156-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamaoncol.2025.2681" pmid="40839273" pmcid="PMC12371547" count="1">156</citation>].

At therapeutic doses, GLP-1 RAs amplify and prolong the GLP-1-mediated effects described above. <sentence_start/>Their principal anti-obesity effects include reduced appetite and hedonic eating, delayed gastric emptying, enhanced satiety, and lower food intake. <sentence_start/>They may also improve leptin sensitivity and energy expenditure. <sentence_start/>In addition, they improve glucose homeostasis through glucose-dependent insulin secretion and reduced glucagon release and may benefit lipid metabolism, adipose-tissue function, and systemic inflammation [<citation rid="B157-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.amjmed.2025.01.021" pmid="39892489" count="1">157</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, beyond their established metabolic effects, GLP-1 RAs show promise in addictive disorders, including alcohol use disorder, by modulating mesolimbic dopamine signaling and reward-driven craving [<citation rid="B158-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2024.4789" pmid="39937469" pmcid="PMC11822619" count="1">158</citation>,<citation rid="B159-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18103/mra.v14i2.7249" count="1">159</citation>].

In dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs, GIP receptor activation complements GLP-1 receptor signaling and may further improve glycemic regulation, lipid metabolism, adipose-tissue function, and metabolic flexibility. <sentence_start/>It may also facilitate switching between carbohydrate and fat utilization, potentially increasing energy expenditure. <sentence_start/>By targeting multiple pathways implicated in obesity and metabolic dysfunction, dual agonists may enhance appetite regulation, glucose metabolism, and body-weight control, helping explain their superior therapeutic efficacy relative to GLP-1 RAs alone [<citation rid="B157-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.amjmed.2025.01.021" pmid="39892489" count="1">157</citation>,<citation rid="B160-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41392-024-01931-z" pmid="39289339" pmcid="PMC11408715" count="1">160</citation>].

Despite their therapeutic benefits, GLP-1 RAs and dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs are associated with several clinical challenges, including gastrointestinal adverse effects, interindividual variability in treatment response, loss of lean body mass, and the potential development of nutritional deficiencies. <sentence_start/>These limitations emphasize the importance of integrating personalized nutritional interventions to enhance treatment tolerability, support metabolic health, and improve long-term therapeutic success [<citation rid="B147-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/obesities5040088" count="1">147</citation>].
7.6.2. <sentence_start/>Management of Gastrointestinal Adverse Effects

Gastrointestinal adverse effects represent the most commonly reported complications of GLP-1 RAs and dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs. <sentence_start/>The most frequent symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal discomfort, bloating, and dyspepsia. <sentence_start/>These adverse events are typically mild to moderate, occur more frequently during dose escalation, and tend to diminish with continued treatment. <sentence_start/>Their development is largely attributed to delayed gastric emptying, altered gastrointestinal motility, and central mechanisms involved in appetite and nausea regulation. <sentence_start/>Higher therapeutic doses have also been associated with a greater likelihood of gastrointestinal intolerance [<citation rid="B161-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm12010145" pmid="36614945" pmcid="PMC9821052" count="1">161</citation>].

Nausea is generally the most common gastrointestinal adverse effect during the early stages of GLP-1-based therapy, particularly during dose increase, and may be exacerbated by large or high-fat meals. <sentence_start/>Nutritional strategies that may relieve nausea include consuming smaller, more frequent meals, eating slowly, avoiding overeating, limiting foods with strong odors or high fat content (e.g., fried foods) and, when needed, consuming bland foods such as crackers or dry toast [<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/15598276251344827" pmid="40452753" pmcid="PMC12125019" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="B161-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm12010145" pmid="36614945" pmcid="PMC9821052" count="1">161</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Ginger may provide additional symptomatic relief because of its antiemetic properties [<citation rid="B162-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamainternmed.2025.1133" pmid="40658429" count="1">162</citation>].

Vomiting is less common than nausea but, if persistent, may lead to dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and reduced dietary intake. <sentence_start/>Patients experiencing vomiting are generally encouraged to prioritize adequate fluid intake and consume small amounts of food at shorter intervals to minimize gastric discomfort. <sentence_start/>Avoiding very large meals and foods that are difficult to digest may further improve symptom tolerability [<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/15598276251344827" pmid="40452753" pmcid="PMC12125019" count="1">6</citation>].

For diarrhea, nutritional management should primarily focus on maintaining adequate hydration and temporarily limiting foods that may worsen gastrointestinal symptoms, including alcohol, excessive caffeine, sugar alcohols, highly processed foods, and certain high-fiber products in individuals with lower gastrointestinal tolerance. <sentence_start/>In some patients, choosing more easily digestible foods and progressively reintroducing dietary fiber may support better gastrointestinal adaptation and symptom improvement over time [<citation rid="B152-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/oby.24067" pmid="38853526" count="1">152</citation>,<citation rid="B161-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm12010145" pmid="36614945" pmcid="PMC9821052" count="1">161</citation>].

Constipation may occur because of delayed gastric emptying, reduced gastrointestinal motility, lower food intake, and insufficient hydration. <sentence_start/>Personalized dietary approaches typically emphasize adequate fluid intake, gradual optimization of dietary fiber according to individual tolerance, and regular physical activity. <sentence_start/>Incorporating fiber-rich foods progressively, rather than abruptly increasing fiber consumption, may help minimize bloating and improve bowel regularity during therapy [<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/15598276251344827" pmid="40452753" pmcid="PMC12125019" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="B152-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/oby.24067" pmid="38853526" count="1">152</citation>,<citation rid="B161-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm12010145" pmid="36614945" pmcid="PMC9821052" count="1">161</citation>,<citation rid="B162-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamainternmed.2025.1133" pmid="40658429" count="1">162</citation>].
7.6.3. <sentence_start/>Nutritional Considerations During GLP-1-Based Therapy

Lean body mass preservation and maintenance of adequate nutritional intake have emerged as important considerations during GLP-1 RAs and dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs therapy. <sentence_start/>Although these therapies are highly effective for weight reduction, their potent appetite-suppressing effects can substantially reduce spontaneous food intake and compromise macronutrient and micronutrient consumption. <sentence_start/>Nutritional management should therefore extend beyond calorie restriction alone and emphasize individualized energy intake, overall diet quality, balanced macronutrient distribution, adequate fiber and fluid intake, and prevention of nutritional inadequacies. <sentence_start/>Energy intake recommendations should be individualized according to age, sex, body weight, physical activity level, and treatment response, while excessively restrictive dietary approaches may increase the risk of dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, gallstone formation, and inadequate nutrient intake [<citation rid="B152-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/oby.24067" pmid="38853526" count="1">152</citation>,<citation rid="B163-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnut.2025.1566498" pmid="40352260" pmcid="PMC12062175" count="1">163</citation>,<citation rid="B164-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu17233659" pmid="41373949" pmcid="PMC12693348" count="1">164</citation>].

Weight loss achieved with GLP-1 RAs and dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs may involve reductions in lean body mass, although current evidence suggests that these changes are highly variable and do not necessarily reflect clinically meaningful deterioration in skeletal muscle function. <sentence_start/>Some studies indicate that improvements in muscle quality and insulin sensitivity may occur despite decreases in lean mass, suggesting that part of this change reflects an adaptive response to weight loss rather than clinically significant muscle deterioration [<citation rid="B165-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/dom.15728" pmid="38937282" count="1">165</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, preserving lean body mass remains an important consideration, particularly in older adults and individuals at risk of sarcopenia [<citation rid="B166-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.obpill.2025.100228" pmid="41502845" pmcid="PMC12768930" count="1">166</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Notably, bimagrumab, a recombinant human monoclonal antibody targeting activin type II receptors (ActRIIA and ActRIIB), is a promising therapeutic approach for reducing fat mass while preserving lean mass, both as monotherapy and in combination with GLP-1 RAs. <sentence_start/>Preclinical and phase 2 clinical evidence indicates that ActRII blockade may enhance fat loss and attenuate the reduction in lean mass associated with GLP-1 RA therapy [<citation rid="B167-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.molmet.2024.101880" pmid="38218536" pmcid="PMC10832506" count="1">167</citation>,<citation rid="B168-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-026-04204-0" pmid="41772149" pmcid="PMC13004672" count="1">168</citation>].

Nevertheless, adequate, individualized protein intake and regular physical activity are key components of nutritional care during incretin-based therapy. <sentence_start/>While general recommendations suggest a protein intake of approximately 0.8 g/kg/day for adults, higher intakes ranging from 1.0 to 2.0 g/kg/day may be more beneficial during GLP-1-based treatment, especially in older adults and those with sarcopenic obesity. <sentence_start/>Distributing high-quality protein evenly across meals, with approximately 25-30 g per meal, may further support muscle protein synthesis. <sentence_start/>Adequate sources of protein include fish, poultry, yogurt, and legumes. <sentence_start/>In cases of severely reduced appetite, the use of high-protein oral nutritional supplements providing a minimum of 20 g of protein per serving may help meet protein requirements [<citation rid="B147-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/obesities5040088" count="1">147</citation>,<citation rid="B162-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamainternmed.2025.1133" pmid="40658429" count="1">162</citation>,<citation rid="B169-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.obmed.2026.100690" count="1">169</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Resistance training, combined with regular aerobic physical activity, should complement these dietary measures to help preserve lean mass and improve muscle strength during weight-loss interventions. <sentence_start/>Current recommendations include at least 150 min of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise weekly alongside resistance training comprising 2-3 weekly sessions of approximately 30 min each, using free weights or resistance bands [<citation rid="B165-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/dom.15728" pmid="38937282" count="1">165</citation>,<citation rid="B166-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.obpill.2025.100228" pmid="41502845" pmcid="PMC12768930" count="1">166</citation>].

Balanced carbohydrate and fat intake also remains important. <sentence_start/>Severe carbohydrate restriction does not appear necessary for long-term weight management and may unintentionally reduce the intake of fiber-rich foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and whole grains, which provide important micronutrients and cardiometabolic benefits. <sentence_start/>Similarly, healthy dietary fats are important for the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and maintenance of overall nutritional status during rapid weight loss. <sentence_start/>Emphasis should therefore be placed on unsaturated fat sources such as nuts, seeds, olive oil, avocado, and fatty fish, while limiting fried foods and foods rich in saturated fats that may exacerbate gastrointestinal symptoms [<citation rid="B152-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/oby.24067" pmid="38853526" count="1">152</citation>].

Adequate dietary fiber intake and hydration further support gastrointestinal health, cardiometabolic regulation, and prevention of constipation. <sentence_start/>Fiber should be increased gradually and according to tolerance, with supplementation considered if dietary intake remains insufficient. <sentence_start/>Because reduced appetite and altered thirst perception may contribute to inadequate hydration, regular fluid intake, primarily water and low-calorie beverages, should be encouraged, while alcohol and excessive caffeine are limited [<citation rid="B152-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/oby.24067" pmid="38853526" count="1">152</citation>,<citation rid="B166-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.obpill.2025.100228" pmid="41502845" pmcid="PMC12768930" count="1">166</citation>].

Micronutrient status also requires attention, as individuals with obesity may have suboptimal intake before treatment and appetite suppression can exacerbate deficiencies. <sentence_start/>Patients receiving incretin therapies may fail to meet recommended intakes of vitamins A, D, E, K, and B-group vitamins, as well as calcium, iron, magnesium, and potassium. <sentence_start/>Observational studies report that a substantial proportion develop at least one deficiency within the first treatment year, with vitamin D status frequently affected [<citation rid="B163-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnut.2025.1566498" pmid="40352260" pmcid="PMC12062175" count="1">163</citation>,<citation rid="B164-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu17233659" pmid="41373949" pmcid="PMC12693348" count="1">164</citation>,<citation rid="B170-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/dom.16395" pmid="40259488" pmcid="PMC12146451" count="1">170</citation>,<citation rid="B171-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.obpill.2025.100186" pmid="40584822" pmcid="PMC12205620" count="1">171</citation>].

Personalized dietary strategies should prioritize nutrient-dense, minimally processed foods and balanced meals despite lower energy intake. <sentence_start/>For reduced appetite, early satiety, or gastrointestinal discomfort, smaller, more frequent meals and soft or liquid nutrient-dense options, such as smoothies, soups, yogurt-based products, and protein-enriched beverages, may improve dietary tolerance and facilitate adequate nutrient intake. <sentence_start/>Targeted supplementation, including vitamin D, calcium, and vitamin B12, should be guided by individual nutritional status and clinical need, with regular reassessment of dietary intake, hydration, and micronutrient adequacy throughout treatment [<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/15598276251344827" pmid="40452753" pmcid="PMC12125019" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="B163-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnut.2025.1566498" pmid="40352260" pmcid="PMC12062175" count="1">163</citation>,<citation rid="B164-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu17233659" pmid="41373949" pmcid="PMC12693348" count="1">164</citation>,<citation rid="B166-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.obpill.2025.100228" pmid="41502845" pmcid="PMC12768930" count="1">166</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Figure 2 summarizes the nutritional management strategies for several common adverse effects associated with incretin-based pharmacotherapy.
7.7. <sentence_start/>Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Personalized Dietary Interventions

Recent advances in AI and ML have substantially expanded the potential of precision nutrition by enabling the integration and analysis of large, heterogeneous datasets encompassing genetic profiles, metabolomic signatures, gut microbiome composition, continuous glucose monitoring outputs, dietary intake records, and longitudinal lifestyle parameters. <sentence_start/>Unlike conventional nutritional approaches grounded in population-level dietary recommendations, AI-driven systems are capable of detecting significant interindividual variability in metabolic and postprandial responses to specific foods and dietary patterns, thereby facilitating the development of more personalized and adaptive nutritional interventions. <sentence_start/>Through predictive modeling and real-time data analysis, AI-based technologies can support individualized meal planning, optimization of glycemic control, prediction of pharmacological and dietary treatment response, and improvement of long-term dietary adherence. <sentence_start/>Emerging evidence further indicates that AI-assisted nutritional interventions contribute to clinically meaningful improvements in body weight management, metabolic health, and cardiometabolic risk profiles in individuals with obesity and related metabolic disorders [<citation rid="B175-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnut.2025.1636980" pmid="40771216" pmcid="PMC12325300" count="1">175</citation>,<citation rid="B176-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.obmed.2025.100657" count="1">176</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, AI-driven tools are increasingly being explored as adjuncts to incretin-based pharmacotherapy, offering the potential to tailor nutritional support to the specific metabolic and gastrointestinal challenges associated with GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment [<citation rid="B177-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2196/69466" pmid="40164173" pmcid="PMC11997532" count="1">177</citation>,<citation rid="B178-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2196/63079" pmid="40146920" pmcid="PMC11967752" count="1">178</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Notably, AI is also becoming highly useful in anti-obesity drug discovery, unlocking next-generation therapeutics [<citation rid="B179-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.drudis.2025.104333" pmid="40107411" count="1">179</citation>].

Likewise, AI technologies are being progressively integrated into mobile health applications, wearable monitoring devices, dietary assessment platforms, and virtual coaching systems that enable continuous physiological monitoring and individualized behavioral feedback. <sentence_start/>ML algorithms, image-recognition tools, natural language processing systems, and large language models are facilitating dietary tracking, automating nutritional assessment, supporting behavioral change strategies, and enhancing patient engagement throughout the treatment continuum. <sentence_start/>AI-based approaches also demonstrate considerable promise for identifying maladaptive eating behaviors, anticipating adherence challenges, and dynamically adjusting nutritional interventions in response to evolving physiological and behavioral patterns over time. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, despite this considerable potential, important limitations remain. <sentence_start/>These include concerns regarding data privacy and security, algorithmic transparency and interpretability, equitable access across diverse socioeconomic and ethnic populations, and the limited external validation of AI models in real-world clinical settings. <sentence_start/>Addressing these challenges will require robust, large-scale, and longitudinal clinical studies, as well as the development of standardized regulatory frameworks for AI-driven nutritional tools, before their widespread implementation in routine obesity care can be responsibly recommended [<citation rid="B180-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/healthcare13121417" pmid="40565444" pmcid="PMC12193492" count="1">180</citation>,<citation rid="B181-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/healthcare13202579" pmid="41154258" pmcid="PMC12563881" count="1">181</citation>].
8. <sentence_start/>Current Limitations and Future Perspectives

While precision nutrition and omics-based strategies offer unprecedented opportunities for individualized obesity care, several significant limitations must be addressed before widespread clinical implementation can be achieved. <sentence_start/>First, the high costs associated with omics profiling (genomics, metabolomics, microbiome sequencing) and advanced continuous monitoring devices currently restrict their accessibility, often limiting these interventions to research settings or affluent populations [<citation rid="B182-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnut.2022.979665" pmid="36118748" pmcid="PMC9481417" count="1">182</citation>,<citation rid="B183-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s41669-023-00461-8" pmid="38113009" pmcid="PMC10883904" count="1">183</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This raises concerns regarding socioeconomic inequalities, as individuals most disproportionately affected by the obesity epidemic may have the least access to personalized care [<citation rid="B184-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15143247" pmid="37513665" pmcid="PMC10385361" count="1">184</citation>].

Furthermore, there is a distinct lack of standardized protocols for data collection, analysis, and interpretation across different healthcare systems. <sentence_start/>The integration of multi-omics datasets remains challenging from both computational and clinical points of view [<citation rid="B185-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mnfr.70293" pmid="41163310" pmcid="PMC12700061" count="1">185</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, while several short-term studies demonstrate the potential of personalized nutrition, there is a scarcity of long-term randomized controlled trials validating the sustained clinical efficacy and cost-effectiveness of these approaches compared to standard care [<citation rid="B186-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/ajcn/nqac237" pmid="36055772" pmcid="PMC9761773" count="1">186</citation>].

Looking forward, the successful translation of precision nutrition into routine practice will require the development of multidisciplinary obesity care models that integrate dietitians, geneticists, endocrinologists, and psychotherapists [<citation rid="B182-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fnut.2022.979665" pmid="36118748" pmcid="PMC9481417" count="1">182</citation>,<citation rid="B187-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41366-018-0092-3" pmid="29795471" count="1">187</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Integrating these tools into primary care will depend strongly on user-friendly digital health platforms and AI tools capable of synthesizing complex data into actionable advice for both practitioners and patients [<citation rid="B185-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mnfr.70293" pmid="41163310" pmcid="PMC12700061" count="1">185</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Finally, clear clinical guidelines, robust practitioner training, and stringent ethical frameworks regarding genetic privacy and AI-driven healthcare data will be essential to ensure that precision nutrition is delivered in a safe, equitable, and effective manner [<citation rid="B188-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18231/j.ijnmhs.82717.1769060072" count="1">188</citation>,<citation rid="B189-nutrients-18-02691" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tjnut.2026.101547" pmid="42013964" count="1">189</citation>].
9. Conclusions

The management of obesity is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving from generalized calorie-restriction models toward highly individualized, multi-dimensional strategies grounded in the biological heterogeneity of the disease. <sentence_start/>This review highlights that the evidentiary strength of precision nutrition varies across its pillars. <sentence_start/>Genetic profiling offers clear utility for monogenic obesity but limited translational benefit when used to match diet type to common polygenic variants, though genetic information may still improve outcomes when leveraged for risk disclosure and engagement rather than strict genotype-diet matching. <sentence_start/>Similarly, microbiome-targeted studies reveal that the <italic>Bacillota</italic> to <italic>Bacteroidota</italic> ratio shows inconsistent associations with obesity across studies, with genus-level and functional alterations offering more reproducible targets. <sentence_start/>Metabolomic approaches to personalized glycemic response have progressed from foundational predictive models toward large-scale clinical validation, while lipidomic pathway analyses offer additional, underutilized avenues for individualized guidance. <sentence_start/>Chrono-nutrition emerges as a promising but still underexplored pillar warranting further investigation.

The integration of personalized nutrition is also crucial in the era of advanced obesity pharmacotherapy. <sentence_start/>As incretin-based obesity medications become central to clinical care, tailored dietary strategies are essential to mitigate gastrointestinal adverse effects, ensure adequate micronutrient intake, and preserve lean body mass during weight loss. <sentence_start/>Looking forward, artificial intelligence and machine learning will be instrumental in translating complex multi-omics and lifestyle data into actionable, real-time nutritional guidance. <sentence_start/>Despite current challenges related to data privacy, algorithm validation, and equitable access, precision nutrition holds the potential to redefine obesity care, offering more effective, sustainable, and evidence-based, patient-centered therapeutic outcomes.

These conclusions, however, should be interpreted in light of the methodological approach adopted in the present review. <sentence_start/>The review is subject to several limitations inherent to its narrative design. <sentence_start/>First, as a non-systematic narrative review, it does not follow a pre-registered protocol or a PRISMA-based selection process, and consequently it is more susceptible to selection and citation bias than a systematic review or meta-analysis. <sentence_start/>Second, the literature search was restricted to publications available in English, which may have excluded relevant evidence published in other languages. <sentence_start/>Third, the findings were synthesized qualitatively, without quantitative pooling of effect sizes, meaning that the conclusions drawn should only be interpreted as a critical, integrative overview of the field rather than a precise, statistically weighted estimate of effect. <sentence_start/>These limitations should be considered when interpreting the conclusions of this review, and future systematic reviews and meta-analyses are warranted to quantitatively confirm the trends discussed herein.
